q: Toluene is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> in the dark. What is the major product?
h: FeBr<sub>3</sub> means a polar ring substitution. CH<sub>3</sub> is an ortho/para director; which of those positions is less crowded?
w: With a Lewis acid and no light, Br2 substitutes on the ring. CH3 is a weak activator that directs ortho/para; the para position is free of steric interaction with the methyl group, so 4-bromotoluene is the major product (2-bromotoluene is the main minor product).
x: CH<sub>3</sub> donates electrons to the ortho and para positions; the meta product forms only in trace amounts.
Benzylic bromination is a radical reaction (light or NBS/peroxide); FeBr<sub>3</sub> in the dark gives ring substitution.
Only one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> is used, so monobromination is the main outcome.

q: What is the major product when methyl benzoate is nitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 0 °C?
h: Which atom of the ester is bonded to the ring, and is it electron-rich or electron-poor?
w: The CO2CH3 group is attached through its δ+ carbonyl carbon; it withdraws electrons by resonance and induction. Ortho/para attack would place the ring cation next to that carbonyl carbon, so substitution occurs meta: methyl 3-nitrobenzoate. The product ring is even more deactivated, so a second nitration does not occur at 0 °C.
x: Para attack gives a σ complex with the cation on the carbon bonded to the electron-poor C=O carbon; it is disfavored.
Ortho attack has the same destabilized form as para attack, plus steric hindrance.
After one nitro group the ring is doubly deactivated; dinitration needs much harsher conditions.

q: What is the major product of this Friedel–Crafts acylation?
h: OCH<sub>3</sub> directs ortho/para, the acylium–AlCl<sub>3</sub> electrophile is bulky, and an acyl group deactivates the ring it joins.
w: OCH3 is a strong ortho/para director. The bulky acylating complex strongly prefers the open para position, giving 4-methoxyacetophenone. The C=O introduced deactivates the product, so acylation stops after one group, and the acyl group is not reduced to an alkyl group by AlCl3.
x: OCH<sub>3</sub> donates a lone pair to the ortho and para positions; meta attack gets no such help.
Friedel–Crafts acylation gives a ketone; turning C=O into CH<sub>2</sub> needs a separate Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner step.
The first acyl group deactivates the ring, so a second acylation does not occur (unlike Friedel–Crafts alkylation).

q: 4-Nitrotoluene is nitrated further with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Find the carbon that is ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> and also meta to NO<sub>2</sub>.
w: CH3 (at C1) directs to its open ortho positions, C2 and C6. NO2 (at C4) directs meta to itself, also C2 and C6. The two groups reinforce each other, so the product is 2,4-dinitrotoluene.
x: Substitution ortho to NO<sub>2</sub> (C3) is meta to CH<sub>3</sub> and ortho to the deactivating nitro group; neither group favors it.
TNT requires a third nitration under much harsher conditions; each nitro group makes the next substitution slower.
Nitration with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> substitutes ring C–H, not the benzylic C–H of the methyl group.

q: 4-Methylanisole is treated with one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: The two groups send the electrophile to different carbons. Which group is the stronger activator?
w: OCH3 directs to its ortho positions (para is taken); CH3 directs to its own ortho positions. These are different carbons, so the directors compete, and the stronger activator wins: lone-pair resonance from oxygen beats hyperconjugation from CH3. Bromine enters ortho to OCH3: 2-bromo-4-methylanisole.
x: This is ortho to the weaker activator (CH<sub>3</sub>) and meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>; the σ complex gets no oxygen lone-pair stabilization.
Benzylic bromination needs radical conditions (NBS, light); FeBr<sub>3</sub> gives ring substitution.
With only one equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub>, monobromination is the main result.

q: m-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene) is mononitrated. What is the major product?
h: Three ring positions are activated by both methyl groups or by one. Which of the doubly activated positions is easiest to reach?
w: C2 (between the methyls), C4 and C6 are each ortho or para to both CH3 groups; C5 is meta to both. C2 is flanked by two methyl groups, so attack there is sterically hindered: groups meta to each other block the carbon between them. C4/C6 (equivalent) is ortho to one methyl and para to the other and open, so 2,4-dimethyl-1-nitrobenzene is the major product.
x: C2 is electronically activated by both methyls, but it sits between them; this crowded position gives only a minor product.
C5 is meta to both methyl groups, so neither activator helps the σ complex.
The question asks for mononitration; a second nitro group is not introduced under these conditions.

q: What is the major product when N-(4-methylphenyl)acetamide reacts with Br2 in acetic acid?
h: Both groups direct ortho to themselves. Compare a nitrogen lone pair (even one shared with C=O) with a methyl group.
w: The para position is blocked, so each group directs ortho to itself. NHCOCH3 is a moderate activator (nitrogen lone pair), stronger than CH3 (weak activator). The stronger activator controls: bromine enters ortho to the acetamido group.
x: Ortho to CH<sub>3</sub> is meta to NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>; the stronger activator does not stabilize that σ complex.
Benzylic bromination requires radical conditions; Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid is a polar ring bromination.
N-Bromoamides are not the stable product of Br<sub>2</sub>/AcOH with an activated ring; ring C-bromination is observed.

q: 1-Bromo-4-nitrobenzene is heated with Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
c: no reaction: a ring with two deactivating groups cannot be brominated
h: Br directs ortho/para; NO<sub>2</sub> directs meta. Is there a carbon both groups agree on?
w: Br at C1 directs to C2/C6 (para is taken); NO2 at C4 directs meta to itself, also C2/C6. The directors reinforce, giving 1,2-dibromo-4-nitrobenzene. The ring is deactivated, so heat is needed, but halogenation still occurs.
x: The carbon ortho to NO<sub>2</sub> is meta to Br; bromine's lone pair cannot stabilize that σ complex and the nitro group disfavors it.
Replacing NO<sub>2</sub> by Br (ipso substitution) is not a normal EAS outcome; the electrophile replaces H<sup>+</sup>.
Deactivated rings, even nitrobenzene itself, are brominated with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> and heat; only Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on strongly deactivated rings.

q: 1-tert-Butyl-4-methylbenzene is mononitrated. What is the major product?
h: Both groups are alkyl activators of similar strength. When electronics nearly tie, what decides?
w: CH3 and C(CH3)3 are both weak ortho/para activators; the para positions are mutually blocked, so each directs ortho to itself. Electronically they are similar, so sterics decide: the carbons next to the huge tert-butyl group are hindered, and nitration occurs ortho to the methyl group.
x: Attack next to the bulky tert-butyl group is sterically hindered and gives only a minor product.
HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> nitrates ring C–H bonds, not benzylic C–H bonds.
The question asks for mononitration; the first nitro group deactivates the ring toward a second substitution.

q: 3-Methoxybenzaldehyde reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in acetic acid. What is the major product?
h: Let the activator choose among its ortho/para positions; then eliminate the most crowded one and compare the rest.
w: OCH3 (strong activator) controls over CHO (deactivator). It directs to C2, C4 and C6 (numbering the ring from CHO at C1, OCH3 at C3: its ortho carbons are C2 and C4, its para carbon is C6). C2 lies between the two substituents and is sterically blocked. C4 is ortho to OCH3 and para to CHO; C6 is para to OCH3 and ortho to CHO. Attack para to the activator, where its lone-pair donation is most effective and the electrophile is farther from OCH3, is preferred: 2-bromo-5-methoxybenzaldehyde.
x: This carbon is meta to OCH<sub>3</sub>; following the deactivating CHO group's meta preference ignores the stronger director.
This carbon is between the two substituents (meta to each other), the most hindered position on the ring.
This carbon (ortho to OCH<sub>3</sub>) is electronically allowed, but attack para to OCH<sub>3</sub> is favored; this is the minor isomer.

q: 4-Methylbenzoic acid is nitrated. At which labeled carbon does substitution mainly occur?
c: neither; the CO<sub>2</sub>H group prevents nitration
h: Ask each substituent separately where it sends the electrophile.
w: CH3 directs ortho to itself (para is occupied): that is carbon b. CO2H is a meta director: the carbons meta to it are also b (and its mirror). The directors reinforce, so nitration occurs at carbon b, giving 4-methyl-3-nitrobenzoic acid.
x: Carbon a is ortho to the deactivating CO2H and meta to CH3; neither group favors it.
The two carbons are not equivalent; both substituents favor b.
CO<sub>2</sub>H deactivates the ring but does not stop nitration; it only blocks Friedel–Crafts reactions.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into 4-bromoaniline as the major product?
c: 1. (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, pyridine  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH  3. NaOH, H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
1. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  2. Br<sub>2</sub>, FeBr<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, heat
h: NH<sub>2</sub> is so activating that it is hard to stop at one bromine. How can you temporarily tone it down without changing its directing effect?
w: Free NH2 activates the ring so strongly that bromination runs to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Converting it to the acetamide pulls part of the N lone pair onto C=O: still an ortho/para director, but moderate, and the bulky group favors para. After monobromination, basic hydrolysis removes the acetyl group to give 4-bromoaniline.
x: Unprotected aniline is brominated at all three ortho/para positions even with limited Br<sub>2</sub>; a clean mono product is not obtained.
In excess acid aniline becomes anilinium ion, a meta director, so bromination would favor 3-bromoaniline.
Diazotization replaces the amino group (step 3 would make a phenol), so the target amine is lost.

q: Which compound gives the largest para : ortho product ratio on mononitration?
h: All four are ortho/para-directing alkyl groups of similar electronic strength. What differs?
w: All four alkyl groups activate and direct ortho/para with similar electronic effects, so the ortho share is set by sterics. The bulkier the group, the more it blocks its neighbors. The tert-butyl group is the largest, so tert-butylbenzene gives the highest para : ortho ratio; toluene gives the most ortho product.
x: Isopropyl is bulky but has a benzylic H and can rotate it toward the ring; it hinders the ortho positions less than tert-butyl.
Ethyl is only slightly larger than methyl; ethylbenzene still gives a lot of ortho product.
Methyl is the smallest alkyl group; toluene gives the most ortho product of the four.

q: Biphenyl reacts with one equivalent of CH<sub>3</sub>COCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What is the major product?
h: A phenyl substituent can share its π electrons with the σ complex. Where does that help, and which of those positions is open?
w: A phenyl group is a weak activator and ortho/para director: in the ortho and para σ complexes the positive charge can be delocalized into the second ring. The bulky acylium–AlCl3 electrophile avoids the crowded ortho position (next to the other ring), so 4-acetylbiphenyl is the major product. The ketone deactivates its ring, and one equivalent of reagent gives monoacylation.
x: Meta attack cannot delocalize the cation into the second ring; it gets no help from the phenyl substituent.
The ortho position is electronically allowed but crowded by the other ring, a poor fit for the bulky acylating complex.
With one equivalent of acyl chloride, monoacylation is the main result; the acetyl group also deactivates the molecule.

q: Phenyl benzoate is mononitrated with HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the major product?
h: Decide first which ring reacts: one is bonded to an oxygen, the other to a carbonyl carbon.
w: The ring bonded to the ester oxygen (–OCOPh) is activated: the O lone pair donates into it (moderately, because it is shared with C=O), so this ring reacts and directs ortho/para. The ring bonded to the carbonyl carbon is deactivated. Nitration therefore occurs on the O-bearing ring, mainly para (less hindered): 4-nitrophenyl benzoate.
x: This is the meta product on the deactivated acyl ring; that ring reacts much more slowly than the oxygen-bearing ring.
Right ring, wrong position: the –OCOPh group directs ortho/para on its own ring, not meta.
The acyl ring is deactivated by the C=O, and even if it reacted it would be meta, not para, substituted.
